# SK1001 — Use a collection expression

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A declaration whose type is written out does not need the type written again in `new`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 12.0 |
| Since | 1.2 |
| ReSharper | `UseCollectionExpression` (`resharper_use_collection_expression_highlighting`) |
| Supersedes | IDE0028, IDE0300, IDE0301 |

## Why

`List<string> names = new List<string> { "a" };` says `List<string>` twice, and the second one is the compiler's job. A collection expression takes its meaning from the target type, which here is the type the author already wrote on the left of the `=`. The rule is deliberately narrow because collection expressions are the opposite of the usual modernization: they have no natural type, so `[…]` is legal in some positions and not in others, and an analyzer that fires everywhere fires where it does not compile. This one fires only where an explicit declared type stands beside the initializer and the created object's type is that type exactly.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
string[] names = new string[] { "a", "b" };
List<int> ids = new List<int> { 1, 2 };
```

Write:

```csharp
string[] names = ["a", "b"];
List<int> ids = [1, 2];
```

## When it does not fire

None known. It is silent on `var`, because a collection expression has no natural type and `var x = […]` is CS9176; on any target that is not an array or `List<T>`, because an interface target lets the compiler choose the implementation and identity would change; wherever the created type differs from the declared type in any way, because `object[] a = new string[] { … }` is an array of `string` at run time and `[…]` would make it an array of `object`; where the creation has constructor arguments, because `new List<T>(capacity)` records an allocation decision the rewrite loses; on dictionary-style `{ k, v }` element pairs and on object initializers; and inside an expression tree. ⚠ One difference is real and accepted: `List<T> x = […]` may be built with an exact capacity where `new List<T> { … }` grows, so `x.Capacity` can differ. The elements, the type and the identity do not.
